title: Knowledge Check 5: Lessons 21-25
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 21-25 of the hermes-consultant-intermediate series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Why should an agent pipeline validate its input shape and stop rather than continue when the input changes?
options: Because stopping reduces the number of model tokens each run consumes
Because a loud failure is cheaper to diagnose than quiet wrong output
Because validation removes the need for any human to review the output
Because source schemas are guaranteed never to change again once matched
questions.explanation: The tempting failure mode keeps producing output that looks fine, which is worse than stopping. Designing for a loud, dated failure makes the problem cheap and visible instead of shipping wrong drafts.

questions.question: When a defect in the client's own data surfaces mid-build, what is the professional response?
options: Absorb the cleanup into the engagement because you are already working in the data
Quietly work around it without telling the client to avoid a difficult conversation
Name the defect with evidence, refuse to own it, and build a workaround
Pause the engagement entirely until the client fixes the data themselves
questions.explanation: Absorbing a pre-existing client defect costs unpaid days, teaches that exclusions are soft, and hides a governance problem. Naming it with evidence and pricing a workaround keeps ownership where it belongs.

questions.question: Against what should the value of a delivered engagement be measured at the close?
options: Against a definition agreed before the change, reported honestly
Against the final state of the system the agent happens to have produced
Against the vendor's own dashboard activity metrics for the run period
Against whichever improvement looks strongest in the final week of the engagement
questions.explanation: Measurement needs a definition that predates the change, so the agreed metric is the one reported. Reporting the smaller, verifiable number builds a claim the buyer can check and trust.

questions.question: What makes a strong checklist item?
options: A broad reminder that restates the plan for the current phase
A step that has failed before and fails silently when it is dropped
A long list that covers every task in the framework from start to finish
A description of the desired outcome rather than any specific step
questions.explanation: A checklist is a pre-mortem device, not a to-do list. It names the high-consequence step whose failure is silent and should stay short enough to be consulted under pressure.

questions.question: What distinguishes a useful template from a blank form?
options: It has more fields and longer sections for the next person to fill in
It is stored in a shared tool that the whole team can reach at once
Each field carries the reasoning a past engagement learned to ask
It is reviewed and approved by the client before the engagement begins
questions.explanation: A blank form gives boxes with no guidance, while a real template encodes the questions earlier work paid to discover. That captured reasoning is what makes it transferable and worth versioning.

questions.question: What turns a sequence of phases into a repeatable, priceable delivery framework?
options: Defined outputs and gates before work moves to the next phase
A detailed timeline that lists every task in chronological order
A flexible plan the consultant reinvents for each new client engagement
A fixed method that is never revised once it has been written down
questions.explanation: Gates are where variation gets caught early and where a failure becomes cheap and visible. A known process with known outputs is estimable and priceable in a way an improvisation is not.

questions.question: Which kind of number belongs in a report to the buyer?
options: The number of sessions and tokens the agent consumed over the period
The business effect the buyer would have paid for without the agent
The uptime percentage of the agent's runtime environment
The number of successful runs the scheduler completed this month
questions.explanation: Activity metrics describe the machinery and tell the buyer nothing they can act on. A number is worth reporting only when it maps to something the buyer would have paid for anyway.

questions.question: When must the baseline for an outcome metric be captured, and why?
options: At the end of the engagement, drawn from the client's memory of the old process
Whenever it is convenient once the agent is already running in production
Before the solution exists, from the client's real data, agreed in writing
Only if the buyer later requests a formal before-and-after comparison
questions.explanation: A baseline reconstructed after delivery gets idealized in memory, which makes it contested. Freezing it in writing from real data before the solution exists keeps the comparison honest.

questions.question: How should a consultant handle the possibility that another initiative shares credit for an improvement?
options: Name it first and claim only the share the agent can honestly own
Leave it out of the report so the agent's contribution looks larger
Report only a metric for which no other initiative could apply
Wait for the buyer to raise it and then adjust the numbers afterward
questions.explanation: The buyer will think of the other initiative anyway, so naming it first and conceding its weight keeps the claim credible. Claiming only the provable share is what makes the report believed.

questions.question: What are the three capabilities that make up ownership of a delivered system?
options: Reading, writing, and archiving the operating documentation
Running the system, changing it, and passing it to the next person
Monitoring, alerting, and escalating problems back to the consultant
Building, testing, and deploying new versions of the system
questions.explanation: Ownership is operational, change, and sustaining capability together, and each is taught differently. Training only the first leaves a team that is frozen or a single point of failure.

questions.question: What rule separates real training from a demonstration?
options: The training session runs longer than a standard working meeting does
The client receives printed documentation to keep at the end of it
If the consultant operates it, the client is not learning to own it
The training includes a slide deck the client can keep afterward
questions.explanation: A demo is a performance the consultant gives while the client watches, and nothing changes. Real training ends with the client having run the work themselves under coaching, with your hands off the controls.

questions.question: Why should at least two operators be trained to the same standard?
options: So the capability survives one of them leaving or changing roles
So the consultant can bill more hours to the engagement in total
So the two can divide the operational and change work between them
So the second operator can review the first operator's work before it runs
questions.explanation: A single trained person reintroduces the exact single point of failure the handover tried to remove. Two operators at the same standard keep the capability alive through any one absence.

questions.question: What separates a composed set of scope, plan, and estimate artifacts from three documents that are merely stacked?
options: Each artifact is written in the same template and reviewed by the same person
Each artifact improves the other two, so deleting one would weaken the rest
Each artifact is delivered to the client on the same day
Each artifact repeats the others' content so the reader can cross-check them
questions.explanation: The composition test is interdependence: a scope that adds no gate to the plan, or a plan that prices nothing new, is just separate paperwork. Each artifact should strengthen the other two rather than sit beside them.

questions.question: Where should buffers be placed in an engagement plan, and why?
options: As one large cushion in the final week, so recovery is concentrated
Evenly across every week, so no single phase carries more risk
At the points of genuine uncertainty, such as after a technical spike and before handover
Only after the last gate, so the estimate stays a single clean number
questions.explanation: A single end-of-plan buffer moves all risk to the final week, where it cannot be recovered from. Small buffers positioned where uncertainty actually lives absorb surprises where they occur.

questions.question: What makes an acceptance bar clause usable when the work is handed over?
options: A stranger with the test set could grade it without exercising judgment
It is written in the client's own words rather than the consultant's
It is agreed verbally with the sponsor before the build starts
It is restated in the estimate as a line item with a price
questions.explanation: An acceptance clause must be a testable claim: a person with no context and the test set can grade every clause. If a clause needs judgment to evaluate, it belongs in a risk note instead.
